instruction: How to save tax through donations in India under Section 80G?
output: Section 80G allows tax deduction for donations to approved charitable organizations in India: Types of deductions: 100% deduction without limit: PM National Relief Fund. PM CARES Fund. National Defence Fund. Swachh Bharat Kosh. Clean Ganga Fund. Chief Minister Relief Fund. 50% deduction without limit: Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund. Prime Minister's Drought Relief Fund. Rajiv Gandhi Foundation. 100% deduction with qualifying limit: Donations to approved local authorities, institutions, associations. 50% deduction with qualifying limit: Most registered NGOs, educational institutions, medical institutions. Qualifying limit: 10% of adjusted gross total income. Example: Income Rs 10 lakh. Qualifying limit = Rs 1 lakh. Donate Rs 1.5 lakh to NGO (50% category). Deduction = 50% of Rs 1 lakh (limit) = Rs 50,000. Conditions: 1) Donation by cheque/DD/online (no cash for deductions above Rs 2,000). 2) Get stamped receipt with NGO's 80G registration number. 3) Verify 80G registration status at incometax.gov.in. 4) Form 10BE now required from organization. 5) Not available under new tax regime (check latest rules). High-impact causes in India: Give India, Akshaya Patra, Teach For India, GiveDirectly - all have 80G approval. CSR donations from companies also eligible under 80G.

instruction: What are small finance banks in India and are they safe for deposits?
output: Small Finance Banks (SFBs) in India: Established under RBI licensing from 2015-16. Primary focus: Financial inclusion, serving underserved segments. Key SFBs in India: AU Small Finance Bank, Equitas SFB, ESAF SFB, Jana Small Finance Bank, Suryoday SFB, Ujjivan SFB, Unity SFB, Northeast SFB, Utkarsh SFB. Interest rates: FDs: 8-9.5% (vs 6.5-7.5% at large banks). Savings accounts: Up to 7% (vs 2.5-4% at large banks). Why higher rates: Need to attract deposits, competitive pressure. Safety of deposits: 1) Regulated by RBI: Same as other scheduled commercial banks. 2) DICGC insurance: Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank - same as other banks. 3) Capital adequacy requirements: Same stringent norms as large banks. 4) Risk: Higher NPA (Non-Performing Assets) ratio than large banks in some cases. 5) Some SFBs aspire to become universal banks (AU already applied). Risk assessment: Lower risk than NBFCs/cooperative banks, but higher than large PSU/private banks. Strategy: 1) Limit FD in any single SFB to Rs 5 lakh (DICGC limit). 2) Choose SFBs with lower NPA ratios (AU, Equitas better positioned). 3) Higher rates justify some additional risk for Rs 5 lakh deposits. 4) Don't keep all savings in SFBs - diversify with large banks. Most conservative option: SBI + 2-3 SFBs for higher returns on safe amounts.

instruction: How does the Gold Loan work in India and when should you take one?
output: Gold Loan in India - quick credit against gold jewelry/coins: How it works: Pledge gold ornaments/coins at bank or NBFC. Bank assesses purity and weight. Provides loan of 75% of gold value (LTV regulated by RBI). Repay loan + interest to get gold back. Key features: 1) Interest rates: Banks 8.5-12%, NBFCs (Muthoot Finance, Manappuram) 12-24%. 2) LTV: Maximum 75% of gold value (RBI regulation). 3) Tenure: 3-24 months typically. 4) Processing: Extremely fast - 30 minutes to few hours. 5) No credit score requirement. 6) Documents: Just ID proof + gold. 7) Repayment options: Bullet (pay at end), EMI, overdraft (pay interest monthly, principal flexible). Gold loan pros: Fastest loan available. Lower interest than personal loans. No income proof needed. No credit score requirement. Good for short-term emergency needs. Gold loan cons: Risk of gold being auctioned if default. Emotional attachment to ancestral jewelry. Purity assessment may be unfavorable. Best for: Medical emergencies, business cash flow crunch, wedding expenses (temporary), bridging short-term financial gaps. Better than: Personal loans (lower cost), credit cards (much lower cost). Avoid if: You can access cheaper alternatives, gold has sentimental value, long-term need (cost adds up). Best lenders: Banks (SBI, HDFC, Axis) for lower rates. Muthoot/Manappuram for fastest disbursement.
